title: A Tree Full of Life
passage:
An old tree can have holes in its trunk and still be alive. Its inner wood may become soft and break down while the living parts continue to grow. Some young insects eat the soft wood. As the wood breaks down, spaces form inside the tree. Birds can build nests in these spaces, and bats can rest there.

So a tree does not have to look perfect to be useful to wildlife. A trunk with holes may hold more life than a visitor first notices. A tree can also provide a home for animals after it dies. Dead wood is part of a living forest, although the tree itself no longer grows. Removing every dead tree would also remove places where some forest animals live.

explanation: "An old tree can have holes in its trunk and still be alive." Birds can nest in these spaces, and bats can rest there.

wrong3_2: Birds eat their insects; insects eat living leaves.

title: Art in the Dark
passage:
A drawing can disappear from a museum wall without being sold or sent for repair. Works on paper are often displayed for limited periods because light can damage both the paper and the materials used to create the image. Even when visitors notice no immediate change, exposure may be causing harm.

Museums therefore control how brightly sensitive works are lit and how long they remain on display. Returning a drawing to storage reduces further exposure; it does not undo damage already caused by light. A carefully repaired tear is a different matter: conservation treatment can address some physical damage without reversing changes caused by light.

Changing the works on display lets visitors encounter different pictures while limiting exposure for individual objects. The collection can remain intact even when the gallery walls look different.

title: Walking Towards an Idea
passage:
A walk may help when you need ideas, but that does not mean it improves every kind of thinking. In a 2014 study, researchers compared adults' performance on tasks completed while sitting or walking. One task asked for unusual but possible uses for everyday objects. Another required a single word that correctly linked three other words.

Walking helped participants generate creative ideas, but it did not improve performance on the task requiring one correct answer. Some creative benefits also continued briefly after participants sat down again.

Fresh scenery was not necessary for the effect: walking on a treadmill indoors, facing a blank wall, also helped idea generation. These findings support a particular use for walking during creative work. They do not establish that walking improves every stage, from producing possibilities to choosing the best solution.

title: A Place to Begin
passage:
An arts centre that removes entrance fees may attract more visitors without making it easier for beginners to take part. Watching an exhibition and risking a first attempt at drawing are different experiences. A programme can be publicly available yet still assume that everyone arrives with equipment, confidence and spare time.

I would therefore reserve one evening each week for beginners, with materials provided and no requirement to display finished work. Regular workshops could continue on other evenings. This would extend the programme rather than replace it.

An annual exhibition would still be selected on artistic quality. Places in the beginner sessions, however, would be allocated by application order, not by portfolios. These arrangements serve different purposes: the exhibition presents accomplished work; the sessions give inexperienced people somewhere to start. Attendance figures alone would not tell us whether that second purpose had been achieved.

title: A River with Two Homes
passage:
A river can begin high in the hills and end in the sea. A river can pass through many different landscapes during its journey. The land beside it may look quite different near the end from the beginning. On its way, the water carries small pieces of rock and soil. Near the sea, the river may slow down and leave some of this material behind.

Over time, land can build up where the river meets the sea. This area is called a delta. A river may divide into smaller channels there. These channels carry water across the new land. Not every river ends in a delta: some flow into lakes, and some reach the sea without building one.

title: The Moving Mountain of Ice

A glacier is a large area of ice that moves slowly over land. It may look like a motionless white mountain to someone standing nearby. Its movement can be too slow to notice during a short visit. Snow can build up over many years and become ice. As the ice moves, it can carry rocks and change the land beneath it.

The ice at the front of a glacier may melt while ice farther back continues to move forwards. This means that moving ice and melting ice can be part of the same glacier. In warmer weather, water from melting ice can flow away as a stream. A glacier does not need to be completely still for its front to become smaller.

title: The Desert After Rain

Water can move quickly over the dry ground and gather in low places. Later, the riverbed may become dry again. A person visiting only after the water has gone might see no river there. That does not mean water never flows through the place. The amount of rain, rather than temperature alone, is what makes an area a desert.

title: An Invention for Clean Water
passage:
A water treatment system may use several stages to improve water quality. People may need to deal with visible particles and with things too small to see. A useful treatment process must be chosen for the water and the risks involved. One stage can remove larger pieces of material; another may address harmful microorganisms. The exact process depends on the water source and the system.

At a visitor centre, a model shows water passing through different containers. The labels describe the purpose of each stage, but the model itself is not producing drinking water for the town. A visitor assumes that water is safe as soon as it looks clear. The guide explains that appearance alone cannot show whether harmful microorganisms are present. title: The Island Research Trip
passage:

title: A Journey through the Mountains

title: Cooking beside the Sea

title: Under the Northern Lights

title: The Bookshop Journey

title: The Last Canoe
passage:
A youth group was canoeing on a calm lake when the wind became stronger. The students had practised paddling with an instructor before moving away from the landing place. At first, the surface was smooth and the far shore was easy to see. The instructor decided that everyone should return to the shore. Two canoes were close to the landing place, but the third was farther away.

Instead of asking the nearest pair to race back, the instructor told them to stay together and move steadily towards the shore. The more distant canoe followed the same route. The instructor explained that arriving together had not been necessary; keeping the group on a clear route mattered more than making every canoe land at exactly the same time.

title: An Unexpected Role on Stage
passage:
Before the school play, an actor lost her voice. Rehearsals were complete, and families were about to arrive at the hall. Everyone wanted to find a way to present the story despite the last-minute problem. The director asked Hugo, who had been helping backstage, to read the actor's lines from the side of the stage. Hugo did not have time to learn the whole part by heart, so he used a printed script. At first, he was worried that the audience would find the arrangement confusing. The director introduced the change before the performance began. The play continued with the movements and spoken lines shared between two students. Afterwards, Hugo returned the script to the director and helped put the scenery away.

title: Finding the Way in Fog
passage:
During a guided walk, fog covered the path ahead. Earlier that morning, the students had been able to see across the valley. The guide had planned a route with a rest at a viewpoint before returning to the bus. The group could still see the guide and the next path marker, but the distant hills disappeared. One student suggested continuing to the viewpoint because they were already halfway there.

The guide checked the map and explained that the route beyond the next marker crossed uneven ground. With visibility getting worse, the group turned back to a shelter. An hour later, the fog began to lift, but the group did not restart the walk because their bus was due. They used the remaining time to review the route on the map and discuss why the guide had changed the plan.

title: The Deep Pool Demonstration

title: The Storm and the School Broadcast
